Definition: Effectively synthesizes multiple pieces of information.
Emerging: Summarizes information from multiple sources (with citations) but does not integrate the information
Expanding: Integrates information from multiple sources (with citations) to explicitly identify relationships and patterns (e.g., compare/contrast)
Exemplifying: Integrates information from multiple sources (with citations) to form insights and connections beyond information cited from each source

Definition: Evaluates the strength and relevance of evidence used to form a conclusion. Note: Evidence is anything used to support a claim, which can include both facts and opinions / anecdotes.
Below Emerging: Presents evidence but does not link evidence to a specific conclusion and does not evaluate the relevance or strength of the evidence for the argument generated (i.e., evidence is only listed). Note - If there is no specific conclusion provided, this is the highest code when evidence has been provided.
Emerging: Presents evidence and links evidence to a specific conclusion, but does not evaluate the relevance or strength of the evidence for the argument generated
Expanding: Presents evidence and accurately articulates distinctions between weaker and stronger evidence used to form a specific conclusion
Exemplifying: Presents evidence, articulates distinctions between weaker and stronger evidence to form a specific conclusion, and provides an explanation for their evaluation (e.g., why a piece of evidence is stronger or weaker).

Definition: Effectively addresses counterarguments. Note: Counterarguments may also include qualifiers.
Not Applicable: No opposing view(s), counterargument(s), or qualifier(s) acknowledged or no specific conclusion is drawn (e.g., the position of the argument is unclear) and thus it is not possible to determine opposing view, counterargument, or qualifier status
Below Emerging: Acknowledges general or vague opposing view(s),counterargument(s), or qualifier(s) (e.g., â'others may disagreeâ')
Emerging: Acknowledges specific opposing viewpoint(s), counterargument(s) or qualifier(s)
Expanding: Acknowledges opposing viewpoint(s),counterargument(s), or qualifier(s), and develops response(s) to them
Exemplifying: Acknowledges opposing viewpoint(s),counterargument(s), or qualifier(s), evaluates them (refuting them when appropriate or considering them when they are reasonable), and integrates multiple perspectives into a coherent and reasonable argument

Definition: Relies on data and/or facts over opinions. Note: Claims are not considered as facts or opinions.
Not Applicable: Only uses opinions to support claim(s) and/or argument  (no data and/or facts presented)
Below Emerging: Uses more opinions than facts to support claim(s) and/or argument
Emerging: Uses facts and opinions about equally to support claim(s) and/or argument
Expanding: Uses more facts than opinions to support claim(s) and/or argument
Exemplifying: Uses more facts than opinions to support claim(s) and/or argument, including discussion of the source, quality, and/or nature of facts and opinions

Below Emerging: No specific conclusion is drawn (e.g., the position of the argument is unclear)
Emerging: Draws a specific conclusion to analyze simple and straight-forward relationships / argumentations
Expanding: Draws a specific conclusion using valid assumptions (e.g., factually correct claims) to analyze complex relationships / argumentations
Exemplifying: Draws a specific conclusion using valid assumptions to analyze complex relationships / argumentations, and articulates the relationships / argumentations accurately (e.g., assumptions, evidence, claims)

Definition: Recognizes and avoids logical fallacies. Note: Fallacies are common errors in reasoning that will undermine the logic of your argument. Evidence is anything used to support a claim, which can include both facts and opinions / anecdotes.
Not Applicable: Uses only logical fallacies (one type or more) when generating arguments
Below Emerging: Uses more logical fallacies than evidence when generating arguments
Emerging: Uses logical fallacies and evidence about equally when generating arguments
Expanding: Uses more evidence  than logical fallacies when generating arguments
Exemplifying: Uses more evidence than logical fallacies when generating arguments, avoids most or all logical fallacies and articulates the nature of these fallacies (e.g., causation fallacy, false equivalency, etc.)
